Fitting FINN to forest inventory data (Oregon, US FIA)

Source: vignettes/D-Fit_to_FIA.Rmd
D-Fit_to_FIA.Rmd

Dynamic forest models are usually developed through a combination of encoding ecological knowledge into model structures and parameters. Usually the resulting parameters are then further refined by manual calibration procedures. Here we calibrate FINN directly from data: a subset of the US Forest Inventory & Analysis (FIA) program for Oregon, prepared exactly as in the Preparing your data for FINN vignette.

We fit FINN to 200 sites and evaluate on 200 held-out sites.

The calibration needs a torch backend and takes several minutes, so this vignette is precompiled: the code was run once and its output committed with it. The code you see is exactly the code that produced the output next to it.

library(FINN)
library(torch)
library(data.table)
library(ggplot2)

# Training length. Every epoch simulates the 20 years between the inventories
# for all 200 sites; the convergence section below shows the loss curves and how
# far the parameters still move.
EPOCHS <- 500L

The data

The input tables are a seeded sample of 400 Oregon FIA plots with their WorldClim climate, split into 200 sites to fit on and 200 holdout sites for evaluation (?fia_obs_dt). A fitted FINN model should generalize to other sites, so the holdout is a genuine out-of-sample test.

# The tables ship with FINN as datasets (?fia_obs_dt), already in FINN's input
# format, so there is nothing to read or prepare.

# --- training sites --------------------------------------------------------
obs_dt     <- fia_obs_dt        # observations, wide (one column per variable)
env_dt     <- fia_env_dt        # RAW, untransformed climate
init_trees <- fia_init_trees
species_dt <- fia_species_dt

# --- holdout sites: never seen during fitting ------------------------------
obs_test   <- fia_obs_test
env_test   <- fia_env_test
init_test  <- fia_init_test

cat(sprintf("train: %d sites | holdout: %d sites | %d species | inventory years %s | env years %d-%d\n",
            uniqueN(obs_dt$siteID), uniqueN(obs_test$siteID), uniqueN(obs_dt$species),
            paste(sort(unique(obs_dt$year)), collapse = " & "), min(env_dt$year), max(env_dt$year)))
#> train: 200 sites | holdout: 200 sites | 11 species | inventory years 10 & 20 & 21 | env years 1-22
species_dt
#>     species            species_name
#>       <int>                  <char>
#>  1:       1   Pseudotsuga menziesii
#>  2:       2         Pinus ponderosa
#>  3:       3          Pinus contorta
#>  4:       4          Abies concolor
#>  5:       5           Abies grandis
#>  6:       6      Tsuga heterophylla
#>  7:       7       Tsuga mertensiana
#>  8:       8 Lithocarpus densiflorus
#>  9:       9             Alnus rubra
#> 10:      10          Abies amabilis
#> 11:      11                   other

FINN simulates the forest in yearly steps. The first inventory (2001-02) is the starting state at year 0, and the two remeasurements are compared with the simulated stand 10 and 20 years later; one site of each sample had its third inventory a year or two late, at year 21 or 22. Each observation carries period_length, the years since the previous inventory, and its growth and mortality are yearly rates: fit() averages the simulated yearly rates over those years, and sums the simulated recruits over them for reg. Because the intervals differ between a few sites, fit() scores every site over its own window, which it announces when it starts.

unique(obs_dt[, .(siteID, year, period_length)])[, .(sites = .N), by = .(year, period_length)]
#>     year period_length sites
#>    <int>         <int> <int>
#> 1:    10            10   200
#> 2:    20            10   199
#> 3:    21            11     1

The environment is supplied in natural units: with env_autoscale = TRUE (the default) FINN z-standardizes the predictors internally and reuses the same constants at prediction time, so raw values are all we ever pass. It has one row per site and simulated year; the climate here is each plot’s long-term normal, the same in every year.

ggplot(melt(unique(env_dt[, c("siteID", "temp", "prec")]), id.vars = "siteID",
            measure.vars = c("temp", "prec")),
       aes(value)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, fill = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free", labeller = as_labeller(
    c(temp = "Mean~annual~temp~(degree*C)", prec = "Annual~precip~(mm)"), label_parsed)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "sites") + theme_minimal()

Stand abundance, measured as total basal area per plot (summed over species), against the temperature and precipitation gradients:

# total stand basal area per plot: sum over species, averaged over inventories
site_ba  <- obs_dt[, .(ba = sum(ba, na.rm = TRUE)), by = .(siteID, year)][
                   , .(ba = mean(ba)), by = siteID]
site_env <- env_dt[, .(temp = mean(temp), prec = mean(prec)), by = siteID]
grad <- melt(merge(site_ba, site_env, by = "siteID"),
             id.vars = c("siteID", "ba"), measure.vars = c("temp", "prec"),
             variable.name = "gradient")

ggplot(grad, aes(value, ba)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, size = 0.9, colour = "grey30") +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE, colour = "firebrick", linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~gradient, scales = "free_x", labeller = as_labeller(
    c(temp = "Mean~annual~temp~(degree*C)", prec = "Annual~precip~(mm)"), label_parsed)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Total basal area per plot") + theme_minimal()

Initial cohorts

Each simulation starts from the observed first inventory. We build the starting state for both samples, the holdout gets its own cohorts, from its own sites.

Nsp <- max(obs_dt$species)
init_cohorts      <- makeInitCohorts(init_trees, Nspecies = Nsp)
init_cohorts_test <- makeInitCohorts(init_test,  Nspecies = Nsp)
# shared colours for the two model variants, reused by the scatter and ALE panels
model_cols <- c("Process (mechanistic)" = "#1b9e77", "Hybrid (growth = NN)" = "#d95f02")

Fit a Process-FINN

In the fully mechanistic configuration every process keeps its predefined form, while its species and environmental parameters are learned (optimize* = TRUE) and the formula chooses which environmental predictors enter the growth, regeneration and mortality responses. The model is calibrated end-to-end by gradient descent through the entire simulation.

The four processes are FINN’s defaults, written out here only to give each a formula: regeneration_capped() is the default regeneration, a recruitment mean with a fitted carrying capacity K (see The recruitment cap below). All six responses are fitted jointly in one fit() call with the default loss, and this joint fit with the defaults is the calibration we recommend.

We pass two climate drivers rather than all six available. ~. would use every column, but the six are strongly collinear; temp and tempmin correlate at r = 0.93, prec and precwarmq at 0.86, and two principal components carry 90% of the variance. Collinear predictors are not a problem for the fit (that is what ALE is designed for), but they are a problem for the interpretation below: two drivers that correlate at 0.93 have no separately identifiable response curves, so calling each one a “niche” would be reading structure into an arbitrary split. Two weakly-correlated drivers (r = 0.64) give curves that mean what the text says they mean. Measured across three seeds on the earlier ten-year steps, the cost was nothing on growth (0.56 vs 0.55 held out) and ~0.02 on basal area, tree numbers and regeneration.

FINN.seed(42)
m <- finn(
  N_species            = uniqueN(obs_dt$species),
  recruits_dbh         = 12.9,   # DBH (cm) assigned to a new recruit; ~ FIA's 12.7 cm (5 in) minimum
  competition_process  = createProcess(~0, FINN::competition,  optimizeSpecies = TRUE),
  growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::growth,       optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::regeneration_capped, optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::mortality,    optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE)
)

Balancing the six losses

The objective is the sum of six terms, one per response, and their raw magnitudes have nothing to do with each other: dbh is a squared error in cm², growth a squared error on a ratio, trees a Poisson deviance. Before anything is trained it is worth seeing what each term would contribute. fit(epochs = 0) runs the set-up only, the data tensors, the intercept-only baselines and the weights derived from them, and reports each response’s share of the objective; nothing is trained and the parameters stay as they were.

fit(m, env = env_dt, data = obs_dt, init_cohort = init_cohorts, epochs = 0L,
    patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE)
#> ℹ Using per-site aggregation windows (one backward per batch): period_length varies between sites
#> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00202, ba=3.9, trees=0.684, growth=1.91e+04, mortality=19, regeneration=0.588)
#> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=17%, ba=17%, trees=17%, growth=17%, mortality=17%, regeneration=17%

With the default loss_weights = "auto" every loss is divided by its own intercept-only baseline, the loss of predicting the single best constant, so each term starts at 1 and the six shares are equal. The baselines are kept in m$loss_baseline, the weights in m$loss_weights.

A numeric loss_weights vector multiplies these scaled losses (since 0.2.0), so a number reads directly as a share: c(1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1) gives growth twice the weight of every other response, and the report says so.

fit(m, env = env_dt, data = obs_dt, init_cohort = init_cohorts, epochs = 0L,
    patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE,
    loss_weights = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1))
#> ℹ Using per-site aggregation windows (one backward per batch): period_length varies between sites
#> ℹ weights: intercept-only baseline x your vector (dbh=0.00202, ba=3.9, trees=0.684, growth=1.91e+04, mortality=19, regeneration=0.588)
#> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (scaled): dbh=14%, ba=14%, trees=14%, growth=29%, mortality=14%, regeneration=14%

weight_scale = FALSE applies the same vector to the unscaled losses, which is what weights meant before 0.2.0 and what reproduces an analysis fitted with an earlier version. The report is printed in that mode too, and it shows why the scaling is the default:

fit(m, env = env_dt, data = obs_dt, init_cohort = init_cohorts, epochs = 0L,
    patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06, plot_progress = FALSE,
    loss_weights = c(1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1), weight_scale = FALSE)
#> ℹ Using per-site aggregation windows (one backward per batch): period_length varies between sites
#> ℹ share of the objective at the intercept-only baseline (raw scale): dbh=99%, ba=0.052%, trees=0.29%, growth=4.2e-05%, mortality=0.011%, regeneration=0.34%

On the raw scale the diameter term is the objective and the nominal factor of two on growth is a factor of two on a share that was already negligible. Read the printed shares at the start of every fit; a response that holds a fraction of a percent of the objective is a response the fit will not learn.

The fit 

fit(m,
  env         = env_dt,      # raw climate
  data        = obs_dt,
  init_cohort = init_cohorts,
  device      = "cpu",
  epochs      = EPOCHS,
  batchsize   = 40L,
  patches     = 4,
  patch_size  = 0.06,
  lr          = 0.01,
  env_autoscale   = TRUE,        # default
  checkpoints     = 50L,         # record every parameter every 50 epochs (m$param_history)
  plot_progress   = FALSE        # the convergence plot below is the readable one
)

Replace growth with a neural network (Hybrid-FINN)

FINN’s defining feature is that any single demographic process can be swapped from a mechanistic function to a neural network, while the others stay mechanistic, a hybrid model. The mechanistic processes keep the system ecologically constrained; the network absorbs structure the fixed functional form cannot express. Here we replace growth with a small neural network via createHybrid(), leaving competition, regeneration and mortality mechanistic, and refit on the same data with the identical fit() call.

FINN.seed(42)
m_hybrid <- finn(
  N_species            = uniqueN(obs_dt$species),
  recruits_dbh         = 12.9,
  competition_process  = createProcess(~0, FINN::competition,  optimizeSpecies = TRUE),
  growth_process       = createHybrid(~ temp + prec, hidden = c(20L, 20L), transformer = FALSE),  # NN replaces growth
  regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::regeneration_capped, optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::mortality,    optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE)
)
fit(m_hybrid,
  env = env_dt, data = obs_dt, init_cohort = init_cohorts, device = "cpu",
  epochs = EPOCHS, batchsize = 40L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06,
  lr = 0.01, env_autoscale = TRUE, plot_progress = FALSE
)

With both variants fitted, the rest of the vignette inspects and compares them: training convergence, the skill on the training and the held-out sites (evaluate()), a summary() of the fit, the fitted parameters (plot()), a run from bare ground, and the accumulated local effects that reveal what the network learned.

Training convergence

Both variants are trained the same way. Because the losses are scaled by their intercept-only baselines, m$history can be read per response on one axis, and the dashed line at 1 is a real reference: it is the intercept-only model, so a curve below it means that response is predicted better than by its own mean.

hist_dt <- as.data.table(do.call(rbind, m$history))[, 1:6]
setnames(hist_dt, c("dbh", "ba", "trees", "growth", "mort", "reg"))
hist_dt[, epoch := .I]
ggplot(melt(hist_dt, id.vars = "epoch", variable.name = "response"),
       aes(epoch, value, colour = response)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.8) +
  scale_y_log10() +
  scale_colour_viridis_d() +
  labs(x = "epoch", y = "loss / intercept-only baseline\n(1 = no better than the mean)",
       colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

The structural responses drop well below 1 within a few epochs. The per-tree rates sit much closer to it; they are only weakly constrained by two inventories, which is the honest picture and the reason for the caveat further down.

A flat loss is necessary for convergence, not sufficient: the objective can be flat along a direction in which the parameters are still moving, which is what a poorly identified parameter looks like. fit() keeps the parameters of the last 51 epochs, and summary() (below) reports how far each one moved over the last 50. checkpoints = 50 in addition recorded every parameter block every 50 epochs in m$param_history, to compare points of the fit further apart (with folder = "<dir>" the whole model is also written there at each checkpoint, as epoch_<k>model.pt, to resume from with torch::torch_load() and a further fit(), or to compare).

Assess the fit: evaluate()

The fit was calibrated on the 200 training sites, so scoring it there only tells us how well it reproduces them. The honest question is whether it transfers. evaluate() answers both: it simulates the model on the training sites it keeps from fit() and, with holdout, on the 200 held-out sites, each started from its own first inventory and driven by its own environment, and pairs every simulated value with its observation on site × year × species.

The simulation runs in yearly steps, so a prediction is put together the way fit() compares it with an inventory: the stand (dbh, ba, trees) at the year of the census, the yearly growth and mortality rates of the period_length years before it compounded into one rate per year – the geometric mean of 1 + g minus one, and one minus the geometric mean survival, the functional makeObsData() derives the observed rates with – and the expected recruits per hectare (r_mean_ha) summed over those years.

Two optional parts are added here. tree_data, the trees of the holdout inventories (fia_tree_test), adds the largest diameter per site, census and species (dbh_max), a size measure that a few large or many small trees do not shift as much as the mean diameter. bare_ground = TRUE runs the model from an empty stand for years years, under the climate of each of sites held constant: we take the coldest, a middle and the warmest training site. fit(..., holdout = ) would run the same evaluation right after the fit.

site_temp  <- env_dt[, .(temp = mean(temp)), by = siteID][order(temp)]
bare_sites <- site_temp[c(1, .N %/% 2, .N), siteID]   # coldest, middle, warmest

FINN.seed(1)
ev <- evaluate(m,
  holdout     = list(data = obs_test, env = env_test, init_cohort = init_cohorts_test,
                     tree_data = fia_tree_test),
  bare_ground = TRUE, years = 500, sites = bare_sites, patches = 50)
ev
#> FINN evaluation
#> ===============

#>     trees  0.8000       0.895  0.75783  0.04324    1.068 4400    NA

#>       reg -0.0273       0.240  6.15605  0.21111    1.138 4400    NA

The skill measures are R² (1 - SSE/SST, the share of the observed variation the simulation reproduces; it is negative when the observed mean predicts better), the Pearson correlation, the RMSE in each response’s own units, the bias (mean of simulated minus observed) and pred/obs, the ratio of the mean simulation to the mean observation. For mortality the AUC replaces R² as the measure of skill (see Scoring mortality per tree below and the mortality vignette).

plot() draws the comparison on the holdout (set = "train" for the training sites): observed against simulated for the states and growth, with R² in each panel; the ROC curve of mortality, every tree at risk one case; and the ratio of simulated to observed recruitment per species, summed over all sites, because recruitment per site is too noisy for a correlation.

plot(ev)

The same skill per species, type = "heatmap": R² (AUC for mortality) on the left, and the ratio of simulated to observed on the right, white where the two agree, red where the model under- and blue where it overestimates:

plot(ev, type = "heatmap")

Process against hybrid

The hybrid is evaluated the same way. Side by side, R² and RMSE of both models on the training and the held-out sites:

m_hybrid$eval()                                  # deterministic: dropout off
FINN.seed(1)
ev_hybrid <- evaluate(m_hybrid,
  holdout = list(data = obs_test, env = env_test, init_cohort = init_cohorts_test))

skill_of <- function(ev, label)
  rbind(ev$train$skill[,   .(variable, model = label, split = "train",   r2, rmse)],
        ev$holdout$skill[, .(variable, model = label, split = "holdout", r2, rmse)])
comparison <- dcast(rbind(skill_of(ev, "Process (mechanistic)"),
                          skill_of(ev_hybrid, "Hybrid (growth = NN)"))[variable != "dbh_max"],
                    variable + model ~ split, value.var = c("r2", "rmse"))
setcolorder(comparison, c("variable", "model", "r2_train", "r2_holdout",
                          "rmse_train", "rmse_holdout"))
cols <- c("r2_train", "r2_holdout", "rmse_train", "rmse_holdout")
comparison[, (cols) := lapply(.SD, signif, 2), .SDcols = cols][]
#> Key: <variable, model>
#>     variable                 model r2_train r2_holdout rmse_train rmse_holdout
#>       <fctr>                <char>    <num>      <num>      <num>        <num>
#>  1:      dbh  Hybrid (growth = NN)    0.600      0.440    14.0000      14.0000
#>  2:      dbh Process (mechanistic)    0.630      0.460    14.0000      14.0000
#>  3:       ba  Hybrid (growth = NN)    0.940      0.940     0.1200       0.0870
#>  4:       ba Process (mechanistic)    0.940      0.920     0.1300       0.0960
#>  5:    trees  Hybrid (growth = NN)    0.800      0.810     0.7600       0.7700
#>  6:    trees Process (mechanistic)    0.800      0.810     0.7600       0.7800
#>  7:   growth  Hybrid (growth = NN)    0.330      0.200     0.0071       0.0083
#>  8:   growth Process (mechanistic)    0.210      0.300     0.0078       0.0077
#>  9:     mort  Hybrid (growth = NN)    0.032     -0.017     0.1100       0.0910
#> 10:     mort Process (mechanistic)    0.074     -0.026     0.1000       0.0920
#> 11:      reg  Hybrid (growth = NN)   -0.030      0.073     6.2000       6.1000
#> 12:      reg Process (mechanistic)   -0.027      0.091     6.2000       6.0000

# the paired tables of both models, for the sections below
pairs_of <- function(ev, label) rbindlist(list(
  copy(ev$train$matched)[,   `:=`(model = label, split = "train")],
  copy(ev$holdout$matched)[, `:=`(model = label, split = "holdout")]), fill = TRUE)
obs_pred <- rbind(pairs_of(ev, "Process (mechanistic)"),
                  pairs_of(ev_hybrid, "Hybrid (growth = NN)"), fill = TRUE)

Basal area and tree numbers are reconstructed well and hold up on sites the model never saw; the mean diameter is reproduced less well on the held-out sites than on the training sites. The gap between the train and holdout columns is the part that matters, because it is the only evidence that the fitted processes generalise rather than memorise. The noisier per-tree rates (growth, mortality, regeneration) are harder to constrain from two inventories and should be read with that in mind (see the caveat below). The hybrid tracks the mechanistic model on the structural variables, with no growth equation specified, which is what makes hybrids useful when a process’s form is uncertain; the surrounding mechanistic processes still anchor the model ecologically.

A caveat on the rate variables. growth, mort and reg are per-tree rates and are only weakly constrained by two inventories, so their R² is a noisy estimate; refitting with a different random seed moves it by a few hundredths. Differences of that size between the models should not be over-read; the structural variables, estimated from far more information, are what carry the comparison. mort is the extreme case and gets a vignette of its own (Mortality: a binomial response and a neural-network process) because R² and rank correlation are the wrong tools for a response that is mostly zeros; its AUC is the measure to read.

Score what the loss scores

evaluate() pairs on site × year × species, which is the cell the loss is computed on: fit() compares the patch-mean of each site, year and species with the observation, and so does the table. Aggregating the predictions differently before scoring (summing species to a stand total, averaging the two censuses, pooling sites into regions) asks a different and usually easier question, and the number it returns is not the skill of the fitted objective. If a stand total is what matters, score it as well, but say so; and for a count-weighted response weight the metric the way the loss does. The mortality vignette carries this through for the binomial term, whose AUC is weighted by n_at_risk exactly as the likelihood is.

A model-free reference: persistence

An R² of 0.92 on basal area sounds good until it is compared with the simplest forecast available: the previous census of the same site and species, unchanged. On a ten-year interval that persistence forecast is strong for the state variables, and a model has to beat it before it can claim to have learned dynamics rather than inertia. The persistence forecast is no simulation, so it is scored by hand, with the measures evaluate() uses: the second census of the holdout sites predicted by the first, next to the two models scored on the same cells.

r2   <- function(obs, pred) 1 - sum((pred - obs)^2) / sum((obs - mean(obs))^2)
rmse <- function(obs, pred) sqrt(mean((pred - obs)^2))

hold <- obs_pred[split == "holdout" & variable %in% c("dbh", "ba", "trees")]
# the first remeasurement (year 10) stands in as the prediction for the second
# (year 20, or 21/22 where it came late); the observations are the same in the
# tables of both models
obs_hold <- hold[model == "Process (mechanistic)"]
persist  <- merge(obs_hold[year > 10, .(siteID, species, variable, obs)],
                  obs_hold[year == 10, .(siteID, species, variable, pred = obs)],
                  by = c("siteID", "species", "variable"))
ref <- rbind(persist[, .(variable, obs, pred, model = "Persistence (year 10 as is)")],
             hold[year > 10, .(variable, obs, pred, model)])
ref[, .(r2 = round(r2(obs, pred), 2), rmse = signif(rmse(obs, pred), 2)),
    by = .(variable, model)][order(variable, model)]
#>    variable                       model    r2   rmse
#>      <fctr>                      <char> <num>  <num>
#> 1:      dbh        Hybrid (growth = NN)  0.34 16.000
#> 2:      dbh Persistence (year 10 as is)  0.87  6.800
#> 3:      dbh       Process (mechanistic)  0.36 15.000
#> 4:       ba        Hybrid (growth = NN)  0.91  0.110
#> 5:       ba Persistence (year 10 as is)  0.96  0.076
#> 6:       ba       Process (mechanistic)  0.89  0.120
#> 7:    trees        Hybrid (growth = NN)  0.73  0.920
#> 8:    trees Persistence (year 10 as is)  0.89  0.600
#> 9:    trees       Process (mechanistic)  0.72  0.930

Persistence wins on all three state variables, and not narrowly. That is the expected result for a ten-year interval in mature stands: most of the basal area present at the second census was already there at the first, and the models are at a disadvantage here, they start from the year-0 tree list and never see the year-10 census, so their year-20 prediction carries twenty simulated years of compounded error. The lesson is not that the models are poor but that a holdout R² on dbh, ba or trees is mostly a statement about the initial cohorts. The processes are tested by the rates, and by what the model does over horizons where persistence has nothing to say, such as the runs from bare ground below. Persistence has no prediction for the first remeasurement, which is why the table scores the second only.

Calibration: predicted against observed by decile

A scatter shows the spread; it hides a systematic bias of the kind a fitted model develops when it compresses towards the mean. Binning the predictions into deciles and comparing the mean prediction of each bin with the mean observation in it is the calibration view, and it is cheap. Cells in which the species is absent from both the observation and the prediction are left out: they are most of the table and would pile the lower deciles onto zero.

calib <- obs_pred[split == "holdout" & variable %in% c("ba", "trees") & (obs > 0 | pred > 0)]
calib[, bin := cut(pred, unique(quantile(pred, 0:10 / 10)), include.lowest = TRUE),
      by = .(model, variable)]
calib_dt <- calib[, .(pred = mean(pred), obs = mean(obs), n = .N), by = .(model, variable, bin)]
ggplot(calib_dt, aes(pred, obs, colour = model)) +
  geom_abline(slope = 1, intercept = 0, colour = "grey40", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.6) + geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  facet_wrap(~variable, scales = "free") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = model_cols) +
  labs(x = "mean prediction in decile", y = "mean observation in decile", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "top")

Points on the diagonal are calibrated; a slope below one means the model under-predicts the dense stands and over-predicts the sparse ones, a slope above one the reverse. A correlation is blind to either; R² is not, but it does not say which way the error goes.

A blocked holdout

The 200 holdout sites are a random draw from the same region as the training sites, so every holdout site has training neighbours in climate space, and nearly so in geographic space. That split measures interpolation. The question usually asked of a calibrated model, how it does in conditions or places it was not trained on, needs a holdout that is blocked: with coordinates, hold out whole spatial blocks (grid cells, or clusters of plots); without them, hold out a block of the environmental gradient. The bundled sample carries no coordinates, so the block here is environmental, but the recipe is the same. We hold out the warmest fifth of the training sites, fit the same model on the other 160, and score it on the 40 blocked sites and, for comparison, on the 200 random holdout sites.

site_temp <- env_dt[, .(temp = mean(temp)), by = siteID]
warm      <- site_temp[temp > quantile(temp, 0.8), siteID]      # the blocked holdout
cool      <- setdiff(site_temp$siteID, warm)                    # the training block

FINN.seed(42)
m_block <- finn(
  N_species            = Nsp, recruits_dbh = 12.9,
  competition_process  = createProcess(~0, FINN::competition,  optimizeSpecies = TRUE),
  growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::growth,       optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::regeneration_capped, optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::mortality,    optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE)
)
fit(m_block,
  env = env_dt[siteID %in% cool], data = obs_dt[siteID %in% cool],
  init_cohort = makeInitCohorts(init_trees[siteID %in% cool], Nspecies = Nsp),
  device = "cpu", epochs = EPOCHS, batchsize = 40L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06,
  lr = 0.01, plot_progress = FALSE
)

Each holdout is one call of evaluate():

FINN.seed(1)
ev_random  <- evaluate(m_block, holdout = list(
  data = obs_test, env = env_test, init_cohort = init_cohorts_test))
ev_blocked <- evaluate(m_block, holdout = list(
  data = obs_dt[siteID %in% warm], env = env_dt[siteID %in% warm],
  init_cohort = makeInitCohorts(init_trees[siteID %in% warm], Nspecies = Nsp)))
blocked <- rbind(
  ev_random$holdout$skill[,  .(variable, holdout = "random", r2, r, rmse, bias, n)],
  ev_blocked$holdout$skill[, .(variable, holdout = "blocked (40 warmest sites)", r2, r, rmse, bias, n)])[
  variable %in% c("dbh", "ba", "trees", "growth")][
  , `:=`(r2 = round(r2, 2), r = round(r, 2), rmse = signif(rmse, 2), bias = signif(bias, 2))][
  order(variable, holdout)]
blocked
#>    variable                    holdout    r2     r    rmse     bias     n
#>      <fctr>                     <char> <num> <num>   <num>    <num> <int>
#> 1:      dbh blocked (40 warmest sites)  0.44  0.77 20.0000 -1.1e+01   195
#> 2:      dbh                     random  0.42  0.72 15.0000 -5.2e+00  1048
#> 3:       ba blocked (40 warmest sites)  0.92  0.96  0.2100 -2.3e-02   880
#> 4:       ba                     random  0.92  0.97  0.0950 -9.8e-03  4400
#> 5:    trees blocked (40 warmest sites)  0.60  0.83  1.2000  1.6e-01   880
#> 6:    trees                     random  0.77  0.88  0.8600  5.8e-02  4400
#> 7:   growth blocked (40 warmest sites) -0.50  0.39  0.0100  1.7e-03   187
#> 8:   growth                     random  0.27  0.58  0.0079 -2.7e-04  1000

The blocked rows are the transfer skill, and they are the ones to report when the model is meant to be applied beyond the sampled conditions. On the warm block the R² of basal area is 0.92 against 0.92 on the random holdout, with an RMSE of 0.21 against 0.095; for tree numbers the R² is 0.6 against 0.77, and for growth -0.5 against 0.27. Where the R² falls while the correlation of the same cells holds, the model orders the warm sites but misplaces their level, and the bias column says in which direction. That is what an environmental response that is extrapolating looks like, and a random holdout cannot show it. It is also the reason to keep the climate formula small: a response curve fitted to two collinear drivers can fit the training block and still extrapolate in opposite directions.

What the model learned: summary() and plot()

summary() brings the checks of a fit together: the skill that evaluate() stored on the model (without a stored evaluation it evaluates the training sites itself), the convergence of the loss and of the parameters over the last 50 epochs, the bare-ground runs, and for each process and species how important each environmental predictor is (ALE-variance importance, rate-normalised) and its average conditional effect. The conditional effects need a simulation and the local derivatives of every process, which takes long on all 200 training sites, so we compute them on a subset of 30 sites; env and init_cohort choose the sites (without them, all training sites).

xai_sites <- sort(unique(env_dt$siteID))[1:30]
env_xai   <- env_dt[siteID %in% xai_sites]
init_xai  <- makeInitCohorts(init_trees[siteID %in% xai_sites], Nspecies = Nsp)
s <- summary(m, env = env_xai, init_cohort = init_xai)
s

The convergence section answers what the loss curves cannot. The loss has settled when its terms change by a fraction of a percent over the last 50 epochs, the parameters when theirs do too. At a constant learning rate the parameters can keep moving by several percent while the loss is flat: part of that is the jitter of mini-batch Adam, which a learning-rate schedule (control = finnControl(lr_scheduler = "step") or "cosine") damps at the end of a fit, the rest drift along directions the objective does not care about. Two seeds, or two checkpoints, compared on the holdout tell whether such drift reaches the predictions.

plot() of a fitted model draws the fitted parameters themselves, one point per species, on the scale on which they enter the process functions; the dashed lines mark the bounds of a parameter where a species comes near one, and an open triangle a species that ended the fit at a bound:

plot(m)

pars = "env" draws the environmental niches of the processes whose response is linear: the fitted environmental term of every species across the range of each predictor, the other held at its mean. For growth and regeneration a higher curve means faster growth or more recruits, for mortality more deaths:

plot(m, pars = "env")

From bare ground

The bare-ground runs that evaluate() stored start from an empty stand under the climate of the coldest, a middle and the warmest training site, held constant for 500 years. plot(ev, type = "bare_ground") draws them as successions, one panel per site labelled with its climate; outside an evaluation, simulateForest(m, bare_ground = TRUE, years = 500, sites = ...) gives the same run.

plot(ev, type = "bare_ground")

Basal area here is per patch of 0.06 ha, as in the inventory plots. Over the last tenth of the run the three stands hold 0.6 to 8.9 m² per patch (10 to 148 m² per hectare), led by Abies concolor and Abies grandis (the bare-ground table of summary() above). These are long extrapolations from two inventories, and the place to see whether the fitted processes produce a plausible forest at all: a stand that collapses, or one species that takes every site, would show here long before it shows in the skill tables. Here it does: at the warmest site the stand grows to about 148 m² per hectare, with Abies grandis holding 95 % of it, which is not a plausible forest; the skill tables on the held-out sites do not reveal this.

Trajectories against the inventories

simulateForest() returns the whole trajectory, not only the census years. comparePlot(type = "timeseries"), or the same plot(sim, obs, type = "timeseries"), draws it as a line, averaged over the sites, with the observations at their census years as points; species gives one row of panels per species. The holdout sites, for the four most common species:

FINN.seed(1)
sim_test <- simulateForest(m, env = env_test, init_cohort = init_cohorts_test)
comparePlot(sim_test, obs_test, type = "timeseries", species = c(1, 2, 4, 5))

Each panel is the mean over the holdout sites where the species was observed. The line shows what the model does between the censuses, which the scatter plots cannot: whether a species’ basal area and stem numbers rise or fall steadily, and whether the rates the inventories report at year 10 and 20 sit on the simulated course. plot(sim_test) alone draws the simulation without the observations.

Scoring mortality per tree

The mortality term above compares the mean death probability over the simulated cohorts of a site, census and species with the pooled rate of the inventory. That mean carries a compositional confound: mortality changes several-fold from the smallest to the largest trees, so the cell mean moves whenever the simulated size distribution moves, whether or not the hazard function is right. The bundled sample carries every tree behind those counts, fia_tree_dt and fia_tree_test: one row per tree alive at the start of an interval, with its diameter then and its fate. With loss_aggregation = c(mortality = "tree") the mortality term is scored on these trees instead, each at its measured diameter with the light of the observed stand, against its 0/1 fate (see ?finn_loss, Scoring individual trees). Everything else stays as in the mechanistic fit.

FINN.seed(42)
m_tree <- finn(
  N_species            = uniqueN(obs_dt$species),
  recruits_dbh         = 12.9,
  competition_process  = createProcess(~0, FINN::competition,  optimizeSpecies = TRUE),
  growth_process       = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::growth,       optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  regeneration_process = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::regeneration_capped, optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE),
  mortality_process    = createProcess(~ temp + prec, FINN::mortality,    optimizeSpecies = TRUE, optimizeEnv = TRUE)
)
fit(m_tree,
  env = env_dt, data = obs_dt, init_cohort = init_cohorts, device = "cpu",
  epochs = EPOCHS, batchsize = 40L, patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06, lr = 0.01,
  loss_aggregation = c(mortality = "tree"),   # the mortality term on the observed trees
  tree_data        = fia_tree_dt,
  plot_progress    = FALSE
)

predictTrees() runs the same per-tree code path on any tree list, so both fits are scored on the holdout trees the same way: the probability that each of the 10,109 holdout trees dies over its interval, against what happened to it. The AUC needs no weighting here, every tree is one trial. predictTrees() needs env for exactly the sites in tree_data; two holdout sites have no tallied tree at risk, so their climate rows are left out.

auc_binom <- function(p, pos, neg) {
  g <- data.table(p = p, pos = pos, neg = neg)[, .(pos = sum(pos), neg = sum(neg)), by = p][order(p)]
  neg_below <- cumsum(g$neg) - g$neg
  den <- sum(g$pos) * sum(g$neg)
  if (den == 0) return(NA_real_)
  sum(g$pos * (neg_below + 0.5 * g$neg)) / den
}
m$eval(); m_tree$eval()
env_tree <- env_test[siteID %in% fia_tree_test$siteID]   # the sites that have trees at risk
tree_pred <- function(model, label)
  cbind(fia_tree_test, model = label,
        mort_pred = predictTrees(model, tree_data = fia_tree_test, env = env_tree, patch_size = 0.06)$mort_pred)
tp <- rbind(tree_pred(m, "site-level mortality"), tree_pred(m_tree, "per-tree mortality"))
tree_auc <- tp[, .(trees = .N, deaths = sum(died), AUC = round(auc_binom(mort_pred, died, 1 - died), 3)), by = model]
tree_auc
#>                   model trees deaths   AUC
#>                  <char> <int>  <num> <num>
#> 1: site-level mortality 10109    734 0.573
#> 2:   per-tree mortality 10109    734 0.601

Both fits rank the holdout trees alike, AUC 0.573 for the site-level and 0.601 for the per-tree fit: on this sample the per-tree term buys little ranking skill, which is the picture of the mortality vignette, where two censuses carry little transferable mortality signal.

Where the two differ is in the size classes. Predicted and observed yearly mortality of the holdout trees by diameter at the start of the interval, in percent per year (a tree’s interval probability p over period_length years is the yearly rate 1 - (1 - p)^(1 / period_length)):

annual <- function(p, years) 1 - (1 - p)^(1 / years)
tp[, dbh_class := cut(dbh, c(0, 20, 30, 45, 61, 80, 100, Inf),
                      labels = c("13-20", "20-30", "30-45", "45-61", "61-80", "80-100", ">100"))]
observed <- tp[model == "per-tree mortality",
               .(trees = .N, deaths = sum(died),
                 observed = round(100 * annual(mean(died), mean(period_length)), 2)), by = dbh_class]
predicted <- dcast(tp[, .(pred = round(100 * mean(annual(mort_pred, period_length)), 2)), by = .(dbh_class, model)],
                   dbh_class ~ model, value.var = "pred")
size_tab <- merge(observed, predicted, by = "dbh_class")[order(dbh_class)]
size_tab
#> Key: <dbh_class>
#>    dbh_class trees deaths observed per-tree mortality site-level mortality
#>       <fctr> <int>  <num>    <num>              <num>                <num>
#> 1:     13-20  3593    338     0.98               0.84                 1.70
#> 2:     20-30  2866    201     0.72               0.84                 1.08
#> 3:     30-45  1618     93     0.59               0.81                 0.97
#> 4:     45-61   553     34     0.63               0.69                 0.72
#> 5:     61-80   812     45     0.57               0.56                 0.54
#> 6:    80-100   450     16     0.36               0.50                 0.45
#> 7:      >100   217      7     0.33               0.31                 0.22

The site-level fit reproduces the pooled rate of a cell and leaves the shape over size to the simulated size distribution: for the trees below 20 cm it predicts 1.7 % a year against the observed 0.98 %, for the trees above 100 cm 0.22 against 0.33 %, the large-tree arm of the size response that site-level rates leave unidentified. Scored per tree, the same hazard function predicts 0.84 and 0.31 % in these two classes and stays within a factor of 1.4 of the observation in every class. Neither route is calibrated in every class; compare the columns class by class.

The recruitment cap, and why stem counts hinge on a few bursts

Regeneration is the response with the least information in it: 87% of the site × census × species cells record no recruit at all, and a recruit enters at 12.9 cm, so over a ten-year interval it adds little to basal area. The unbounded mechanistic mean rises as exp(env), so a steep climate coefficient could turn a warm, wet site into a burst of hundreds of stems in one year. The default regeneration_capped() bounds it with a Beverton-Holt cap, K m / (K + m): one carrying capacity K (stems per hectare and year) shared by all species, started at the largest observed recruitment per hectare and year and held near it by a weak prior, then fitted with everything else (?regeneration_capped; ?recruitment lists the options). The fitted cap of the joint model:

# the fitted carrying capacity, recruits per hectare and year
K <- exp(as.numeric(m$reg_logK))
K
#> [1] 14.57163
# the largest expected recruitment of a holdout site and species over an interval
max_reg <- ev$holdout$matched[variable == "reg", max(pred)]
max_reg
#> [1] 35.67944

The fitted K is 14.6 recruits per hectare and year. The largest expected recruitment of any holdout site and species over a whole census interval is 36 per hectare, about 3.6 a year, far below the cap: on this sample the cap is a guard rail that the climate response never reaches.

The stem count deserves a closer look, because its skill is the least stable of the three state variables. Recruits are sampled at prediction time (createProcess(sample_regeneration = TRUE), the default), so a cell whose expected recruitment is large can receive a burst in one simulation and nothing in the next. The same model evaluated five times on the holdout with different seeds:

reps <- lapply(1:5, function(s) {
  FINN.seed(s)
  evaluate(m, holdout = list(data = obs_test, env = env_test,
                             init_cohort = init_cohorts_test))$holdout
})
trees_by_seed <- rbindlist(lapply(1:5, function(s)
  reps[[s]]$skill[variable == "trees", .(seed = s, r2 = round(r2, 3), r = round(r, 3),
                                         rmse = round(rmse, 3))]))
trees_by_seed
#>     seed    r2     r  rmse
#>    <int> <num> <num> <num>
#> 1:     1 0.807 0.899 0.783
#> 2:     2 0.801 0.895 0.794
#> 3:     3 0.809 0.900 0.778
#> 4:     4 0.813 0.902 0.771
#> 5:     5 0.812 0.902 0.771

# which cells carry the stem error? those whose predicted recruitment is in the
# top 1 % of the same simulation
burst <- rbindlist(lapply(1:5, function(s) {
  d <- reps[[s]]$matched
  merge(d[variable == "trees", .(siteID, year, species, obs, trees = pred)],
        d[variable == "reg",   .(siteID, year, species, reg = pred)],
        by = c("siteID", "year", "species"))[, seed := s]
}))
burst[, top := reg >= quantile(reg, 0.99), by = seed]
total_sq_error <- burst[, sum((obs - trees)^2)]
burst_tab <- burst[, .(cells = .N, share_of_sq_error = round(sum((obs - trees)^2) / total_sq_error, 2),
                       max_reg = round(max(reg), 1)), by = .(top_1pct_recruitment = top)]
burst_tab
#>    top_1pct_recruitment cells share_of_sq_error max_reg
#>                  <lgcl> <int>             <num>   <num>
#> 1:                FALSE 21780              0.84    11.2
#> 2:                 TRUE   220              0.16    35.8

The 1 % of cells with the largest predicted recruitment carry 16 % of the squared stem error, and the seed-to-seed spread in the stem metrics is the same mechanism at work: a site that receives a burst in one draw and not in the next. That is why a single stems R² on a holdout should not decide between two models whose regeneration differs; compare several seeds, or score the expected stand (sample_regeneration = FALSE at prediction time), and look at the largest predicted recruitment, the tail the cap acts on.

Interpreting the growth process with ALE

ALE() returns the accumulated local effect of every driver on each process, the effect measure of choice when predictors are correlated, because it accumulates local changes within the observed data instead of extrapolating to unrealistic combinations. Running it on both fitted models lets us read what growth responds to and compare the mechanistic process with the neural-network hybrid, across growth’s structural inputs (tree size, light) and its environmental niche (climate). It returns one table per process (growth, mortality, regeneration). Without env and init_cohort it reads the effects over all training sites the model keeps from fit(); as for summary(), we use the 30-site subset, which is much faster.

plot() draws the environmental drivers of the three processes, one line per species, here of the mechanistic model:

ale_proc <- ALE(m,        env = env_xai, init_cohort = init_xai, plot = FALSE)   # mechanistic growth
ale_hyb  <- ALE(m_hybrid, env = env_xai, init_cohort = init_xai, plot = FALSE)   # growth = NN
plot(ale_proc)

The drivers are on the standardised scale the model works on. To compare the two models, we use the growth table of each:


# one tidy table with both variants. Environmental drivers come back on the
# model's scaled axis, so back-transform temp/prec to natural units (deg C, mm);
# the structural drivers (dbh, light) are already on their natural axes.
to_natural <- function(a, model) {
  sc <- as.data.table(model$env_scaling)[, .(var = variable, center, scale)]
  merge(data.table(a), sc, by = "var", all.x = TRUE)[!is.na(center), x := x * scale + center]
}
growth <- rbind(
  to_natural(ale_proc$growth, m)[,        model := "Process (mechanistic)"],
  to_natural(ale_hyb$growth,  m_hybrid)[, model := "Hybrid (growth = NN)"])
growth <- merge(growth, species_dt, by = "species")

One helper plots the growth ALE of both variants for any set of drivers, one panel per species × driver, with independent axes so responses of very different magnitude stay legible side by side:

plot_growth_ale <- function(vars, labs) {
  d <- growth[var %in% vars & species %in% c(1, 2, 4, 5)]   # the four focal species
  d[, var := factor(var, levels = names(labs))]
  ggplot(d, aes(x, ale, colour = model)) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.7) +
    facet_grid(species_name ~ var, scales = "free",
               labeller = labeller(var = as_labeller(labs, label_parsed),
                                    species_name = label_value)) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = model_cols) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "accumulated local effect on growth", colour = NULL) +
    theme_minimal() + theme(legend.position = "top", strip.text.y = element_text(angle = 0))
}

Environmental niches

Because the environmental responses are learned rather than prescribed, each curve is an inferred niche, how a species’ growth scales along a climate gradient. The mechanistic process can bend a curve only as far as its exponential response to a linear climate term allows; the network can shape it freely, so a curve with an optimum inside the sampled range is something only the hybrid can draw.

Read these as illustrations of what ALE recovers, not as settled ecology. The per-species shapes are noisier than the structural responses below; growth is weakly constrained by two inventories (see the caveat above), and the mechanistic and hybrid curves do not always agree, even on the sign of a response. That disagreement is itself informative: where two models trained on the same data diverge, the data are not pinning that response down.

plot_growth_ale(c("temp", "prec"),
                c(temp = "temperature~(degree*C)", prec = "precipitation~(mm)"))

Which drivers matter: feature_importance()

The niches show the shape of each response; feature_importance() gives its magnitude. It permutes each environmental predictor and re-simulates, measuring the resulting increase in prediction error, a re-simulation counterpart to the analytical importance in summary(). Below we read off the importances for the growth process of the four focal species:

FINN.seed(1)
fi <- feature_importance(m, env_dt, init_cohorts, nperm = 20L, seed = 1L,
                         patches = 4, patch_size = 0.06, device = "cpu")
fimp_growth <- merge(data.table(fi$growth)[species %in% c(1, 2, 4, 5)],
                     species_dt, by = "species")
ggplot(fimp_growth, aes(reorder(variable, importance), importance, fill = importance)) +
  geom_col() +
  coord_flip() +
  facet_wrap(~species_name, nrow = 1) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(guide = "none") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "permutation importance (delta error)") + theme_minimal()

The importances are learned per species, not shared: the same driver can carry most of the response of one species and little of another.

Response to size and light: did the network recover the mechanistic form?

The point of a hybrid is to ask which functional form the neural network learned and how it compares to the mechanistic function it replaced. In the mechanistic process growth declines with tree size and increases with light availability, by construction. Where the network recovers the same shape without being given the functional form, the mechanistic form was a reasonable choice; where its curves part from the mechanistic ones, the data do not pin the response down.

plot_growth_ale(c("dbh", "light"),
                c(dbh = "diameter~(cm)", light = "light~availability"))

Each curve spans only the range its own model actually simulates (ALE never extrapolates), so where the process and hybrid cover different ranges, the two models simply place that species in different conditions; the mismatch is information, not an artefact.
